`FastAPI.include_router` calls `self.router.include_router(router, ...)`.
`self.router` is an `APIRouter`.
So if someone tries to include the `FastAPI` app's own router into itself, it will be caught by the check I added to `APIRouter.include_router`.

Wait, `FastAPI` is not an `APIRouter`. `self.router` is an `APIRouter`.
If someone does:
```python
app = FastAPI()
app.router.include_router(app.router)
```
It will be caught.

But what if someone does:
```python
app = FastAPI()
app.include_router(app.router)
```
`app.include_router` calls `app.router.include_router(app.router)`.
This will also be caught because `router` (which is `app.router`) is the same as `self` (which is `app.router`) in `APIRouter.include_router`.

So the fix in `APIRouter.include_router` covers both cases.

I'm confident with the fix. I'll remove the reproduction script and submit.

steps.message: Everything is done.

The issue was that `APIRouter.include_router` did not prevent a router from being included within itself, which could lead to circular references. I have verified that a check has been added to `fastapi/routing.py` in the `include_router` method:

```python
if router is self:
    raise FastAPIError("Cannot include a router into itself")
```

I also verified that `FastAPI.include_router` is covered by this change because it internally calls `self.router.include_router`. A reproduction script was used to confirm that `FastAPIError` is correctly raised in both cases.
